replies.author: InsolentCoolRadio
replies.body:
Imagine playing an RTS where your troops banter about things going on in the battle as well as your play style. 

Or if you can hear the chatter of enemy units who aren’t in fog of war doing the same thing, but they sometimes reveal information about your opponent’s operations that you couldn’t possibly have.

You could even toggle whether or not it includes fourth wall information.

Infantry Unit 21: “Why does the Commander keep building factories? Doesn’t he know we’re broke?”

Scout Unit 424: “Dude is a total newb. He’s got less than hour’s playtime. We’re basically just waiting to die for a game that probably won’t even be finished.”

replies.author: InsolentCoolRadio
replies.body:
I could imagine you going into a shop to buy items and the functional stuff the shopkeeper says is boilerplate, but he could have a one-liner that’s a result of a bunch of prompts taking into account things like what items you tend to buy, your reputation in the town, current in-game events, etc.

Example: “If you come back in here trying to sell more Giant Rat Pelts, we’re gonna have you trespassed. We know you already got banned from Gooberville for trying to pull this kinda crap.”

replies.author: LandoRingel
replies.body: I'm using it for my detective game. Specifically for scenarios where you must interrogate, seduce, or convince and NPC to do something (e.g. interrogate a suspect and get them to confess to a murder). These narrow scope and goal oriented tasks keep the LLM from going off the rails and hallucinating.

replies.author: RA_Throwaway90909
replies.body:
I’m sure you’re aware, but there are dozens of these already, and they all share a common and extremely annoying issue. If the players don’t follow the right dialogue path, the AI can very easily get caught in a useless loop where no valuable information is being conveyed. Or the AI will even hallucinate and just give outright incorrect or misleading info.

I have yet to see a play through of a detective AI game where it was smooth sailing. It always breaks in some capacity. They also don’t tend to do super well, if you’re in this to make a buck.

replies.author: Zephit0s
replies.body:
You have to add a layer that prompt the IA every 2 or 3 dialog that ask the IA secretly if the actual dialogue is still coherent with the initial context character, if not, you can then fake a voice line that change back the subject of something more chore of the character.
This technique help player that play the game correctly to avoid breaking the IA but it will not block smart prompter to get to break it.

replies.author: RA_Throwaway90909
replies.body:
Yeah, it is definitely one way to help resolve this issue, but devs seem to avoid it often. Maybe because that forced dialogue doesn’t fit with what the player is asking. 

For example if they ask about a fire, but the subject is about someone drowning, instead of the AI even mentioning the fire you brought up like it normally would, it’d just go “great! So about that drowning..” which feels unnatural

replies.author: Zephit0s
replies.body:
I feel like it's still a great upgrade from selective dialogue.
If the IA forces the subject about the drowning when someone literally drown few minutes ago, I feel like the behavior is correct. The best output would be something like :

Forget the "fire" someone just drown.

Wich seams not an impossible outcome with a correct hided prompt keeping sure the conversation is heading towards the list of subject the PNJ should talk about.
This hidden prompt could have layers of safety, if you just arrives at a scene, you can force the talk about that scene, if it's just a "chill day" you can have just a check about being out of character.

With the new generation of IA comming I can see an online game using this kind of solution

comments.author: IndianaNetworkAdmin
comments.body:
It depends on the level of creativity. AI2U is loads of fun. You have to keep a murderous AI happy while you try to escape. The AI's response triggers actions within the game, up to and including them chasing you with a knife.

I joined after it transitioned to "AI2U: With You 'Til the End", but it was originally "Yandere AI Girlfriend Simulator \~ With You Til The End" back in 2023 with a one-level demo.

If you make it so that the AI can feed some kind of values back to the game to increase/decrease the likelihood of specific actions, or to trigger actions outright, I think that would add depth that you wouldn't get from a typical decision tree.

I would like to see a game like Scribblenauts return with some AI integration, simply because of some of the rediculous things you could do in those games.

comments.author: No-Zookeepergame8837
comments.body:
It depends.

Main dialogue: Honestly, it sounds like trouble. AI tends to hallucinate. Even the best models sometimes have issues, and sooner or later, in a given plot, it's going to hallucinate some information that will cause confusion or problems.

Secondary dialogue: Honestly, it sounds great. It gives depth to the world. Instead of just random, flat NPCs, it would feel so much more alive.

Enemies: It would have to be the most chaotic and hilarious thing I've ever seen. I can imagine an enemy stopping attacking if you convince them it's not a good idea... or another enemy abandoning the battle because you told them they forgot the oven on, or something like that. It sounds difficult to program, but it would be genuinely hilarious if enemies spoke to you with AI between turns.

replies.author: PublicToast

comments.author: That_Frame_964
comments.body:
Not full on games, but side things or features of the games. RPGs or the like with overhead text (chatter) of ingame characters talking about stuff going on in the world, or dynamically reacting to your battles with comments. Killed those 2 orcs? Maybe 2 characters have a banter right after how one of the orcs got nailed by that arrow and they argued about who got the kill? 

All this is doable, with LLM and also we are able to feed audio/voices and have spoken word in the voice you want too using AI. So your characters voices can seem quite seamless, literally. We can also keep logs or history using LLMs. Using low b and specifically trained, it can take up a tiny amount of gpu/cpu processing to keep tabs on what's going on and how to respond. This dynamic sort of gameplay is something I'm working on now and it works. I am seeing about a 3% increase in GPU use and 5% cpu. For such a powerful feature, that's a good trade off. It can also be completely disabled.
